summary: This RFC extends CalDAV calendar access with a standard way to do scheduling operations on iCalendar-based events and tasks, such as invitations and replies. It defines the calendar-auto-schedule feature.

plainLanguage.summary: It lets calendars send and answer meeting invitations by themselves, so you do not have to email a note to each friend.

questions: what is a caldav scheduling inbox
how does caldav request free busy time
subtitle: How a CalDAV server sends meeting invitations and replies for you when a client saves an event.

tldr.problem: CalDAV let clients store and read calendar data on a server, but it had no standard way to invite people to events, collect their replies or look up when they are busy.
tldr.mechanism: The server watches calendar changes. When a client creates, changes or deletes an event that has an ORGANIZER and ATTENDEEs, the server itself sends iTIP scheduling messages to their Inbox collections and updates their copies. Busy time is requested with a POST to an Outbox collection.
tldr.outcome: This defines the calendar-auto-schedule feature. The RFC says most CalDAV implementations already supported it and expects all new ones to support it by default. It is a Proposed Standard, and RFC 7953 updates it.

today: RFC 6638 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7953. It updates RFC 4791 and RFC 5546, and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Implicit Scheduling for CalDAV
sections.content:
This RFC extends the CalDAV calendar-access feature so calendar users can schedule iCalendar events and to-dos with each other. It reuses the scheduling methods of iTIP (the iCalendar Transport-independent Interoperability Protocol): schedule, reschedule, respond and cancel, plus searching for busy time.

The design is a client/server protocol in which the server sends and processes the scheduling messages. A client only creates, modifies or deletes a calendar component, and that is enough to make the server deliver the right messages. The RFC calls this implicit scheduling.

Some iTIP features are out of scope: publishing, countering, delegating, refreshing, forwarding, and replacing the Organizer. The RFC covers scheduling only between users on a single system, though it says that servers can still exchange messages with external users, for example by iMIP (RFC 6047).
sections.plainLanguage: You just save the event in your calendar. The calendar server does the mailing of invitations and collects the answers, so you never send anything by hand.

sections.title: Inboxes, Outboxes and Principal Properties
sections.content:
A server that supports scheduling MUST support CalDAV calendar-access and advertises calendar-auto-schedule in the DAV response header of an OPTIONS request. The server creates the new collections; clients cannot create or delete them.

A scheduling Outbox collection is the target for busy time requests and carries the privileges that control outgoing scheduling. A scheduling Inbox collection holds copies of incoming scheduling messages, either requests from an Organizer or replies from an Attendee. Inbox messages may share the same UID, because several messages can concern one event. Neither collection may sit inside a calendar collection.

Clients find them through principal properties CALDAV:schedule-outbox-URL and CALDAV:schedule-inbox-URL. If either is missing, the user is not enabled for sending or receiving. The REQUIRED property CALDAV:calendar-user-address-set maps calendar addresses such as mailto URLs to principals. The optional CALDAV:calendar-user-type lets a client search only for people or only for rooms.
sections.plainLanguage: Each person gets a mail slot for incoming notes (the Inbox) and an outgoing tray (the Outbox). The server hands you the address of each.

sections.title: Scheduling Operations
sections.content:
When a calendar object resource is created, modified or removed, the server checks whether it is a scheduling object resource. An organizer resource has an ORGANIZER property in every component that matches one of the calendar owner's addresses. An attendee resource has the same ORGANIZER throughout, not matching the owner, plus an ATTENDEE that does.

The server picks the iTIP method for each attendee. When an Organizer creates an event, an attendee with SCHEDULE-AGENT of SERVER (the default) gets a REQUEST; CLIENT and NONE get nothing. Removing the event sends CANCEL. When modifying, removing an attendee sends CANCEL, and adding one sends REQUEST or ADD. HTTP methods map onto this: a PUT that creates a scheduling resource is a Create, PUT over one is a Modify, and DELETE is a Remove.

Attendees may change only a limited set of data, such as their own PARTSTAT, TRANSP, VALARM components and overridden instances. When an Attendee changes PARTSTAT, or adds an EXDATE to drop one recurrence instance, the server MUST send an iTIP REPLY to the Organizer. The server also resets every other attendee's PARTSTAT to NEEDS-ACTION when the Organizer reschedules.

For recurring events, attendees only learn about instances that include them. A client can use SCHEDULE-FORCE-SEND to make the server send a message it otherwise would not, for example to ask an attendee who declined to reconsider.
sections.plainLanguage: When you add or change a guest on your event, the server notices and sends them a note. If a guest says yes or no, the server tells you.

sections.title: iCalendar Parameters, Headers and Status Codes
sections.content:
The RFC adds three iCalendar property parameters. SCHEDULE-AGENT says who delivers messages: SERVER (the default), CLIENT or NONE. SCHEDULE-FORCE-SEND takes REQUEST or REPLY. SCHEDULE-STATUS records the result of the most recent scheduling message. Servers and clients MUST NOT put these parameters into scheduling messages they send.

Delivery results use new REQUEST-STATUS codes: 1.0 pending, 1.1 sent without knowing about delivery (as with email-based iMIP), and 1.2 delivered. The RFC also lists failure codes: 3.7 unknown calendar user, 3.8 insufficient privileges, 5.1 temporary failure, 5.2 no way to deliver, and 5.3 scheduling with that recipient not allowed.

Three HTTP headers are added. Schedule-Reply (T or F) lets an Attendee delete an event without the server sending a DECLINED reply. Schedule-Tag and If-Schedule-Tag-Match prevent edit conflicts: the CALDAV:schedule-tag changes only on a consequential change, not when another attendee merely replies. If the tags do not match, the server MUST fail with 412 Precondition Failed.
sections.plainLanguage: Little labels on each guest say who should send the note, and what happened to the last note. Other labels stop two people from overwriting each other's edits.

sections.title: Incoming Messages and Busy Time
sections.content:
The server MUST process incoming scheduling messages by the rules of RFC 5546, creating or updating scheduling object resources in the recipient's calendars, and it stores the message in the recipient's Inbox as a signal to the client. For an Organizer's request, the server updates the attendee's matching resource or creates a new one in a calendar collection of theirs. A server MAY support a default calendar through CALDAV:schedule-default-calendar-URL on the Inbox, and MUST reject deleting it.

For an Attendee's reply, the server updates PARTSTAT in the Organizer's copy, sets SCHEDULE-STATUS from the reply's REQUEST-STATUS (or 2.0 if absent), and SHOULD tell the other attendees.

For busy time, a client sends a POST to the user's own Outbox with a VFREEBUSY component and METHOD REQUEST. The reply is an XML CALDAV:schedule-response with one CALDAV:response per user, including the busy time as a VFREEBUSY when successful. The property CALDAV:schedule-calendar-transp decides whether a calendar counts toward busy time (opaque is the default).
sections.plainLanguage: When a note arrives, the server files it in your calendar for you. To check if friends are free, you ask the server and it answers with their busy times.

sections.title: Privileges and Security
sections.content:
Scheduling privileges follow WebDAV access control. On an Inbox, CALDAV:schedule-deliver contains schedule-deliver-invite, schedule-deliver-reply and schedule-query-freebusy. On an Outbox, CALDAV:schedule-send contains schedule-send-invite, schedule-send-reply and schedule-send-freebusy. These let a user choose who may schedule with them and who may act on their behalf, such as an assistant.

Servers and clients MUST use HTTP over TLS for all scheduling operations, clients MUST verify the server by RFC 6125, and servers MUST use HTTP authentication. Servers MUST check that the ORGANIZER matches the calendar owner (to prevent impersonation) and that a new UID does not clash with an existing resource that has a different organizer (to prevent spoofing). Servers MUST limit the cost of large operations and MUST NOT leak one user's private data to another through scheduling messages or errors.
sections.plainLanguage: Locks decide who may put notes in your Inbox or send notes in your name. Everything travels in a sealed envelope (TLS) so nobody can read or fake it.
